body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about Ladder comes from its App Store listing, its own website and pricing page, and recent App Store reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

Most people searching for a Ladder alternative aren't unhappy with Ladder. They've hit one of two walls: the price or the phone. Ladder's entry plan, PRO, costs $29.99 a month or $179.99 a year, and on phones, Ladder is iPhone-only.

It's also well liked. Of its 500 most recent US App Store reviews (October 14 to November 13, 2026), 480 are four or five stars, and 142 of those mention a coach or the coaching. So this isn't an escape guide. It answers the two questions behind those searches: is Ladder worth the money, and what do you use on Android?

Ladder or Kiron: who each is for

  • Stay with Ladder if you want a named coach writing your week, coach-led video and a voice in your ear for every set, and a team in the chat. That's what the price pays for, and Kiron does none of it.
  • Switch to Kiron if you're on an Android phone, or you want a structured plan you pick yourself (one of 36, one you build, or one you paste in), with runs on the same calendar, for {{kiron:price-annual}}.
  • Start with something free if money is the whole problem: Ladder posts a free Workout of the Day on its website, and Boostcamp's free tier includes most of its coach-written programs.

Bottom line: Ladder is worth $179.99 a year if you'll press play and follow your coach most days. If you mainly want a plan to follow and a place to log it, you'd be paying for coaching you skip.

Is Ladder worth $180 a year?

The price only makes sense once you see what Ladder is: coaching, not a log with programs attached. A short quiz places you on one of 23 coach-led "teams," each with its own style (bodybuilding, kettlebells, Pilates with strength, HIIT, hybrid and more). Every Sunday your coach publishes the coming week. You press play and the app runs each session: a video of every movement, the coach's voice in your ear, and timing for every set.

Around that sit Team Chat with your coach and teammates, rep and weight tracking with PR alerts, Apple Watch control, music that turns down when the coach talks, and food logging (calories and macros from a photo, a description or a barcode) included in the price.

What it costs, tier by tier

Ladder's pricing page shows one plan, PRO, paid two ways. Monthly, $29.99: one team, which you can change twice a month. Annual, $179.99 up front (Ladder calls it $14.99 a month): every team, unlimited team changes and unlimited Save & Replay. A year of monthly ($359.88) costs about the same as two years of annual ($359.98), so if you're staying, pay annually.

The App Store also lists three higher tiers the pricing page doesn't mention: PRO+, ELITE and ELITE+. Ladder's site says they add 1:1 coaching and form checks.

Ladder's pricing page shows only PRO; all four tiers appear on its App Store listing. Prices vary by region and offer.

On Kiron's side, the annual plan is {{kiron:price-annual}} ({{kiron:price-annual-monthly}}), and two years comes to {{kiron:two-year-cost}}. There's no monthly plan. The weekly plan is {{kiron:price-weekly}}, which adds up to {{kiron:price-weekly-yearly}} if you stay on it, more than Ladder's PRO annual, so compare the annual plans.

Two things favor Ladder here. Its trial is longer: 7 days, with no payment details taken until it ends, where Kiron offers {{kiron:trial}}. And HSA or FSA money can cover PRO annual (see the FAQ).

So, is it worth it?

It depends on whether you'll use the coaching. Ladder's happy reviewers talk about their coaches, often by name. Price comes up in 5 of the 20 reviews at three stars or lower; one 3-star reviewer in November wrote that "the monthly rate of 29.99 is more than the cost of a gym membership." If you'll press play and follow along most days, you're using what you pay for. If you'd rather pick your own exercises, skip the audio or plan around runs, much of it goes unused.

Is Ladder on Android?

No. Ladder's own site says there is no Android app, and its FAQ says Ladder isn't on Android yet, pointing to a waitlist with no date. On phones it's iPhone-only; it also runs on iPad.

On an Android phone, the closest thing is Ladder's web app at joinladder.com/app, which covers workouts, team chat and the training journal in a browser. Ladder calls the iPhone app the full product; food logging, for one, isn't in the web app.

For an actual Android app, you need a different one. Kiron runs on {{kiron:cell-platforms}}. So do Boostcamp, with a large free library of written programs, and Hevy, a workout log whose Pro plan can build a lifting program for you.

Who Ladder is worth it for

Plenty of people. Stay if:

  • You want a person to tell you what to do. A named coach writes your week, new every Sunday. Kiron has no coaches: its plans come from its library, its AI builder or whatever plan you bring.
  • The coaching in your ear is the point. Ladder talks you through each set over a video of the movement. Kiron shows an animated demo for most exercises and runs a rest timer, but nobody talks you through anything.
  • You train better with a team. Ladder has Team Chat on every plan, and 1:1 Coach Chat with form checks on higher tiers. Kiron has no feed, chat or followers.
  • You control workouts from an Apple Watch. Ladder works hands-free from the Watch. Kiron has no Watch app; it reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect after a workout.
  • You want food logging in the same app. Ladder includes calorie and macro tracking. Kiron doesn't track food.
  • You'd pay with HSA or FSA money. Ladder offers that for PRO annual through a partner; Kiron doesn't.

A structured plan without the coach: where Kiron fits

Ladder gives you a plan, a coach to follow and a team. Kiron (that's us) covers only the plan, and handles it differently.

You choose where the plan comes from

Tap Add a program and you get four ways in:

  • Choose a preset program: 36 ready-made programs, filtered by goal, days, equipment and level, from Beginner 5×5 and Novice Linear Progression to hypertrophy splits, kettlebell and bodyweight plans, and Beginner 5K through Marathon.
  • Build one with Kiron: answer a few questions and it designs a program.
  • Import a plan: paste one from ChatGPT, Claude, a coach or a website, or take a photo of it. Kiron turns it into a schedule with sets, reps and rest, phases included. It doesn't open PDFs or spreadsheets, so copy the text or take a screenshot.
  • Start from scratch: pick your days and add your own exercises.

Whatever you pick runs on the training days you choose, on a calendar. Ladder works the other way: its site says programs are designed for a whole team rather than each member, and that it's a poor fit if you want a workout generator. In fairness, Ladder has added some flexibility. Since late August you can move rest days and do two sessions in a day, and a November 4 update lets you customize a workout before it starts and save your own blocks. The plan underneath is still the coach's.

The day can change without the plan changing

Open a workout and tap Adjust today's workout:

  • Change the duration. Fit it into less time and Kiron drops extras, pairs accessories into supersets, then trims accessory sets, keeping the main lifts. Stretch it and it adds sets where your week is behind.
  • Different equipment today, or one tap for a saved gym like a hotel or a garage: Kiron swaps anything that needs gear you don't have.
  • Add to today: core, arms, shoulders, glutes, calves, a cardio finisher or stretching.

Each change is for today only, with Undo, and you can swap a single exercise for today or from now on. Miss a workout and Today shows it with Move to a day, Pick a day or Skip; miss several and you get Push plan back, Pick days or Skip them.

Runs and recovery in the same app

Ladder is strength-first. Some teams mix in cardio (Movewell pairs beginner strength with running, per Ladder's site), and its FAQ says many members add cycling, yoga or other cardio on their own. Kiron puts runs, rides, swims and rows on the same calendar as your lifting, with time and distance, from Beginner 5K to Marathon, plus Sprint Triathlon, Cycling Base and Run + Lift. It doesn't show running pace. Here's how to space running and lifting in one week.

Kiron's recovery map shows which muscles are fresh and which are still recovering, and counts runs, rides and ski days that other apps (Apple Fitness or Slopes, say) save to Apple Health or Health Connect over the last 10 days. When today's workout leans on tired muscles, it tells you why and offers an easier session. We didn't find a recovery view in Ladder's listing or on its site.

What you'd give up

Kiron has no coach, no coach video or audio, no team or chat, and no food logging. It has no Apple Watch app either. What it has is the plan and the log: last time's numbers, the next weight picked from last time, generated warm-up sets, a plate calculator, a rest timer, and about 1,500 exercises, most with an animated demo. It's also new, with a small user base. And it can't bring in your Ladder history (it imports from Fitbod, Strong and Hevy), so your log would start fresh.

Ladder FAQ

Is Ladder on Android?

No. Ladder's site says there's no Android app, and its FAQ offers a waitlist without a date. Its web app works in a browser, without the full feature set. Kiron runs on {{kiron:cell-platforms}}.

How much is Ladder per month?

PRO is $29.99 a month, or $179.99 a year up front, which Ladder presents as $14.99 a month. The App Store also lists PRO+ at $34.99, ELITE at $44.99 and ELITE+ at $49.99 a month.

Is Ladder worth it?

If you'll use the coaching, the reviews are on its side: 480 of its 500 most recent US App Store reviews are four or five stars. If you mainly want a plan and a log, the apps above cover that for less.

Is there a free app like Ladder?

Not with Ladder's coaching. Ladder posts a free Workout of the Day on its website. Boostcamp's free tier includes 99 of its 132 coach-designed programs, on iPhone and Android, as written plans with a log. {{kiron:free-tier-sentence}}

Can I cancel Ladder during the free trial?

Ladder says it collects no payment details until the 7-day trial ends, and that PRO monthly can be cancelled any time in the App Store (on an iPhone: Settings, your Apple Account, Subscriptions). And Kiron? {{kiron:cta-sentence}}

Can I pay for Ladder with HSA or FSA money?

Ladder says yes. Through a partner called Flex, qualifying customers can pay for PRO annual with HSA or FSA funds and a letter of medical necessity. Eligibility varies by provider, so check with your plan administrator. Kiron has no HSA or FSA option.

Where to go from here

If Ladder's price or the missing Android app is why you're here, and a structured plan matters more to you than a coach, try Kiron: pick one of the 36 programs or paste the plan you already follow. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If you'd miss the coach in your ear and the team, Ladder is the right call, and its 7-day trial asks for no payment details, so try it first. If you want an Android app that writes a lifting program for you, Hevy Pro's Trainer does that for $23.99 a year (see Hevy vs Kiron). For an app that plans each workout for you, see how Fitbod compares, or browse apps for following a program by the job they do.
